Dryopteris x australis forms a substantial, upright-arching clump of glossy, dark green, semi-evergreen fronds that hold up well through summer heat and humidity, making it one of the most reliable large ferns for southeastern gardens. Because it is a sterile hybrid it produces no viable spores and will not self-sow or become weedy, spreading only slowly by an expanding crown, which makes it a well-behaved choice for a shaded border or woodland garden where a bold, non-invasive fern is wanted. It tolerates heavier soil and more summer moisture than many ferns and needs little care beyond removing old fronds in late winter before new growth emerges.

Cyathea cooperi is a fast-growing, dramatic tree fern from Australia with a slender, fibrous trunk topped by a crown of large, lacy, arching fronds up to 10 feet long, creating an instant tropical, prehistoric look in a shaded courtyard or lush understory planting. It is one of the fastest-growing tree ferns in cultivation, adding a foot or more of trunk height annually under good conditions, but its speed comes with a need for consistent moisture and high humidity, since the trunk itself absorbs water. In marginal zones, wrap the fibrous trunk with burlap or frost cloth ahead of hard freezes, or grow it in a large container that can be moved to shelter for winter.

Dicksonia antarctica is a slow-growing but exceptionally cold-tolerant Australian tree fern with a thick, shaggy, fibrous trunk and a broad crown of dark green, leathery, arching fronds, forming a striking specimen for a sheltered shaded courtyard or woodland garden. It grows more slowly than Cyathea species, typically only an inch or two of trunk per year, but tolerates cooler, more temperate conditions and light frost better than most of its tropical relatives, making it the tree fern of choice for gardeners at the cooler edge of tree-fern-growing range. Keep the growing crown watered from above regularly, especially in dry weather, since the trunk has no true root system and absorbs much of its moisture through the fibrous trunk itself.

This curious heirloom Victorian-era cultivar of lady fern produces narrow fronds reduced to small, round, bead-like pinnae strung along the frond like lace tatting, an oddity that has been passed down by division among fern collectors since the nineteenth century rather than reproduced reliably from spores. Its small, dainty scale and unique texture make it a conversation-piece specimen for a shaded rock garden, trough, or the front of a fern collection, though it lacks the vigor and fullness of standard lady fern cultivars. Divide clumps carefully in spring to propagate, since the cultivar does not come true from spores and must be maintained vegetatively.

directions: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Siebold's wood fern is slow to establish and slow to spread, so allow it a couple of seasons to settle in before expecting a full, mature clump. Dryopteris sieboldii is an unusual East Asian fern that looks nothing like a typical feathery fern — its stiff, leathery, evergreen fronds are divided into just a few broad, undivided, strap-like leaflets radiating from the frond tip, giving the whole plant a bold, almost palm-like texture. This coarse, architectural form makes it a striking textural contrast to lacy ferns like maidenhair or Japanese painted fern in a shaded border or fern collection, and its thick, leathery fronds are notably more drought- and heat-tolerant than most woodland ferns once established. It spreads slowly to form a tidy clump and needs little maintenance beyond removing any winter-damaged fronds in early spring.
